summary.text: A volcanic winter is a drop in global temperatures after a large, sulfur-rich, highly explosive eruption, when sulfuric acid droplets dim the Sun and make Earth more reflective.
Sulfur gases injected into the stratosphere turn into sulfuric acid droplets within about a week, and these cool the surface for several years.
Feedbacks between the air, ice and ocean can keep the climate cool long after the droplets are gone, possibly for centuries or longer.

facts.label: Cooling agent
facts.value: Sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) aerosols in the stratosphere

facts.label: Aerosol decay time
facts.value: An e-folding decay time of about a year

facts.label: Sky signs
facts.value: Bishop's rings, odd twilights and dark lunar eclipses

facts.label: Size is no guide
facts.value: Eruption size does not predict how severe the cooling is

items.prompt: Volcano A blasts out an enormous volume of rock and ash but little sulfur. Volcano B is smaller but releases a lot of sulfur dioxide. Which is more likely to chill the globe?

options.label: A, because bigger eruptions always cool more
Neither, since eruptions cannot change climate
B, because the cooling comes from the sulfur
Both equally, since only the ash cloud matters

items.explain: Cooling comes from sulfuric acid droplets formed from sulfur gas, and eruption size does not track how much SO₂ comes out, so size does not predict cooling.

items.prompt: A big eruption darkens the sky with ash for days. Why doesn't that ash cause years of global cooling?

options.label: Most of it falls to the ground within weeks
It absorbs heat and warms the air instead
It dissolves into sulfuric acid at once
It is blown out into space by the eruption

items.explain: Most volcanic ash settles within a few weeks and affects only the local area; it is the sulfur gas that forms long-lasting aerosols.

items.prompt: An eruption's sulfur gases stay in the lower atmosphere and never reach the stratosphere. What happens to the droplets they form?

options.label: They spread worldwide and last for decades
They drift up later and cool for several years
They turn into ash and fall near the volcano
Rain washes them out within a few days

items.explain: If the SO₂ stays in the troposphere, the resulting droplets last only a few days because precipitation removes them efficiently.

items.prompt: Scientists propose that some volcanic cooling lasted centuries, long after the acid droplets had cleared. What could keep the chill going?

options.label: Ash layers that stay in the sky for centuries
Spreading ice reflects more sunlight, cooling further
The volcano keeps erupting at a steady rate
The Sun dims for a long time after an eruption

items.explain: Cooling lowers the snowline and lets sea ice and glaciers grow, which cools the ocean and raises surface reflectivity, a loop that can keep the cold going.

items.prompt: While the ground cools after a large sulfur-rich eruption, what happens to the stratosphere where the droplets sit?

options.label: It cools even more than the surface
It stays exactly as it was
It fills with snow clouds
It warms up for several years

items.explain: The aerosols cool the surface by reflecting sunlight but warm the stratosphere by absorbing heat radiated from Earth, for several years.

items.prompt: An old chronicle describes a dim sun, strange twilight colors and an unusually dark eclipse of the Moon. Why would climate scientists care?

options.label: These hint at a volcanic winter at that time
These show the Sun's output was rising
These prove a large meteor struck the Moon
These record unusually warm summers

items.explain: Sulfate aerosols cause solar dimming, odd twilight colors and dark lunar eclipses, so historical records of these events point to volcanic winters.

paragraphs.heading: What a volcanic winter is
paragraphs.text: A volcanic winter is a drop in global temperatures after a large, highly explosive eruption rich in sulfur. Droplets of sulfuric acid veil the Sun and raise Earth's albedo, meaning it reflects more of the incoming sunlight. An eruption throws out both ash and gas, but most of the ash settles within a few weeks and affects only the nearby area for a short time. The climate effect depends mainly on how much sulfur gas reaches the stratosphere.

paragraphs.heading: From gas to droplets
paragraphs.text: Once in the stratosphere, the sulfur gases react with other molecules to form sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, within about a week. These aerosol droplets cool the surface by reflecting sunlight, while warming the stratosphere by absorbing heat radiated from Earth. They can spread around the eruption's half of the globe within weeks and linger: their e-folding decay time is roughly a year, so their effect can last several years. If the gas stays lower, in the troposphere, rain clears the droplets out within a few days.

paragraphs.heading: Size is not what counts
paragraphs.text: The season, the volcano's latitude and how high the gas is injected all shape how the cloud spreads and what it does to climate. Aerosols from eruptions outside the tropics clear out sooner than those from tropical ones, but they stay in one hemisphere, which strengthens the effect there. Records from past eruptions show that the size of an eruption does not predict how hard it cools the climate. That is because bigger eruptions do not necessarily release more sulfur dioxide.

paragraphs.heading: Signs in the sky
paragraphs.text: The sulfate droplets scatter sunlight, which creates striking effects in the sky. These include a dimmed Sun, coronae also called Bishop's rings, oddly coloured twilights, and dark total eclipses of the Moon. People wrote these sights down, and such records, some from before the Common Era, are clues that a volcanic winter was under way.

paragraphs.heading: When the cold feeds itself
paragraphs.text: Some scientists propose that the cooling can outlast the first few years by decades or even millennia, long after the droplets are gone. In the first years the aerosols can cool things enough to lower snowlines widely, so sea ice, ice caps and glaciers spread fast. Oceans then cool and the surface becomes more reflective, which helps the ice spread further in a strong self-reinforcing loop that can hold the cold for centuries or more. Clusters of large eruptions close together have been proposed as triggers or boosters of cold spells such as the Little Ice Age and the Younger Dryas.

paragraphs.heading: Reading the record
paragraphs.text: Tree rings, historical accounts of dust veils and ice cores confirm that some of the coldest years of the past five millennia were caused directly by huge volcanic releases of sulfur dioxide. For earlier times in the Holocene, frost rings in trees that line up with large sulfate spikes in ice cores flag severe volcanic winters. One much-debated case is the Youngest Toba Tuff eruption from Toba Caldera 74,000 years ago, the largest known eruption of the Quaternary. Polar ice cores from that time show four aerosol events that may come from it, with estimated stratospheric sulfate loads of 219 to 535 million tonnes.
